fields.quote: For ARC-AGI, the scores of the CoT models are taken from the official leaderboard 29 , while for Sudoku and Maze, the scores are obtained by evaluating through the corresponding API.
fields.reason: Official-leaderboard scores for the CoT comparators are an external evaluation by others, which the definition explicitly counts as third-party. API evals of Sudoku/Maze are the authors' own, but one external leaderboard is enough for YES.

claims.quote: Standard architectures saturates, failing to benefit from increased depth. HRM overcomes this fundamental limitation, effectively using its computational depth to achieve near-perfect accuracy.
claims.reason: Intro states hierarchical convergence as their coined ARCH mechanism that avoids rapid RNN convergence. Figure 2 compares whole architectures (HRM vs standard/recurrent Transformers), not with-vs-without the mechanism at matched size/data/tokens, so PARTIAL not YES.

claims.quote: we must first introduce two key elements of our proposed method: deep supervision and adaptive computational time.
claims.reason: Authors explicitly call deep supervision (per-segment loss with detached hidden state) a key element of their training method, so it is a TRAIN contribution. No with-vs-without comparison appears in the paper, so ablation NO.

claims.quote: Figure 5 presents a performance comparison between two HRM variants: one incorporating ACT and another employing a fixed computational step count equivalent to ACT's Mmax parameter.
claims.reason: ACT/Q-learning halting is named as a key element of their method (TRAIN), including inference-time scaling via Mmax. Figure 5 is with vs without ACT but does not state matched data/tokens and the step budgets differ, so the lower code PARTIAL.

This restates the same hierarchical-convergence contribution already kept as A_only0 (the process they term on p.3 and elaborate on p.5), not a second distinct ARCH novelty. Drop to avoid double-counting; no separate controlled ablation exists.
